curriculumDefinition.commandsAndConcepts: No new command families. Choosing between a structural change, a bounded range, a protected move, a repeat, and a substitution; matching the reach of an edit to the number and ambiguity of its sites; taking a range from a boundary the file already states; protecting text across intervening deletes; comparing a chosen solution with a working alternative by clarity, setup cost, repeatability, and risk
curriculumDefinition.learningOutcome: Complete a staged edit on realistic code by selecting a mechanism before touching the keys, and justify the selection against an alternative that also works
curriculumDefinition.representativeExercises: Repair an argument list with a text object, a till-motion, and a protected move; rename a local through five uses and the same token through a longer file; restore a joined chain, a reflowed paragraph, and a numbered list; anchor a recording so an irregular row stops or is skipped; count and confirm a pattern before committing it; relocate two snippets across deletes that would overwrite them; edit only the lines a predicate selects; return to each correction site by position rather than by pattern
curriculumDefinition.priorityAndPortability: Integration rather than instruction. Every command here is already taught in Units 1–15 and every capstone closes by comparing its solution with a mechanism that also reaches the target

lessons.title: Capstone: function calls and arguments
lessons.objective: Repair four argument lists in one module by choosing between a structural edit, a register move, and a repeated change.

activities.title: The job at the call sites
activities.body: One module opens three connections and one audit. The environment name is wrong in three places, the audit takes an argument it no longer accepts, and its two remaining arguments are in the wrong order. Nothing here is a new command; the work is deciding which of the tools you already have fits each of the four edits.
activities.grammar: read the shape of the edit, then pick the tool that matches it
activities.contrast: A substitution rewrites matching text anywhere; a text object rewrites one structure exactly where you are standing.

activities.title: Choose the tool before touching the keys
activities.prompt: Two arguments inside one call have to swap places, and the same call also holds a quoted value that appears correctly elsewhere in the file. What handles the swap?

options.label: Delete one argument into a named register and put it back on the other side
A file-wide substitution matching both argument names
A recorded macro replayed over the call

activities.explanation: Reordering is movement, not replacement. A substitution can only rewrite text where it matches, so it cannot carry one argument across another, and it would reach identical text elsewhere in the file that is already correct. A macro would work but pays a recording cost for a single call site. Lifting the argument into a named register keeps it intact while the surrounding punctuation is cleaned up.

activities.title: Point the first connection at staging
activities.instruction: The first connection should name the staging environment instead of the production one. Leave every other line untouched.

commandGroups.explanation: Change the quoted argument as one structure, wherever it sits on the line.
Enter the replacement value.
Return to Normal mode.

checkpoints.caption: The quotes stay; only their contents are gone.

hints: The quotes are part of the structure you want to keep.
A text object finds its delimiters forward on the line, so the cursor does not have to be inside them yet.
Use `ci"`.

feedback.success: The first connection now names staging.
feedback.why: The quoted string is a structure, so a delimiter text object described the edit exactly without counting characters.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: typescript gives a realistic call site whose quoted argument sits among unquoted ones.

activities.title: Remove the trailing audit argument
activities.instruction: The audit call still passes a third argument that the function no longer accepts. The call should end after its second argument.

commandGroups.explanation: Jump to the end of the call so the search for its last separator runs backwards.
Land on the separator that opens the argument being removed.
Delete up to the closing parenthesis, taking the separator and the argument but leaving the bracket.

checkpoints.caption: Standing on the separator makes the rest of the argument one motion away.

hints: Deleting the argument alone would leave a stray separator behind.
A backwards character search reaches the last separator without counting the ones before it.
Use `$F,` and then `dt)`.

feedback.success: The audit call now passes two arguments.
feedback.why: A till-motion stopped short of the closing bracket, so the operator removed the argument and its separator in one range and left the call's structure intact.
feedback.contrast: Deleting a word would have left the separator and the space behind.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: typescript keeps the removed flag visually distinct from the two arguments that remain.

activities.title: Swap the audit arguments
activities.instruction: The audit call should take the environment name first and the host second, with the separator and spacing intact.

commandGroups.explanation: Move onto the first argument.
Lift the argument into a named register instead of the unnamed one.
Remove the separator and space the argument left behind.
Move to the closing bracket, where the argument now belongs.
Open the new separator before the bracket.
Insert the argument straight from the named register.
Return to Normal mode.

checkpoints.caption: The named register holds the argument; the unnamed register does too, for now.
Deleting the separator overwrote the unnamed register — and the named one is untouched.

hints: The separator has to be cleaned up between lifting the argument and putting it back.
Whatever cleans up the separator will overwrite the unnamed register, so the argument needs somewhere safer to wait.
Lift it with `"cdt,` and put it back with `Ctrl-r c` from Insert mode.

feedback.success: The audit call reads environment first, host second.
feedback.why: A named register carried the argument across the edit that would otherwise have destroyed it, so the move survived the clean-up in between.
feedback.contrast: The unnamed register held the argument at first and held only the deleted separator two keys later.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: typescript makes the two argument kinds — an identifier and a quoted literal — easy to tell apart after the swap.

activities.title: Finish the remaining environment names
activities.instruction: Two quoted environment names still read production. Both should read staging, and the timeout constant's name must not change.

commandGroups.explanation: Search for the quoted value, so the identifier that merely contains the same letters is never a match.
Make the first change, which also becomes the change that repeats.
Jump to the remaining match.
Repeat the same change there.

checkpoints.caption: The search skipped the identifier on the second line.

feedback.success: Both remaining environment names read staging, and the timeout constant is untouched.
feedback.why: Including the quotes in the search made the pattern describe the structure, not just the letters, and repeating one change is cheaper than describing it twice.
feedback.contrast: A pattern of the bare word would have matched the timeout constant as well.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: typescript places a lookalike identifier one line above the real matches, which is what makes the precise pattern matter.

activities.title: What the file-wide substitution would have cost
activities.instruction: Watch the rejected mechanism run on the same module and check every line it touched.

commandGroups.explanation: Open the command line.
Replace the word everywhere in the file, which is the whole appeal and the whole risk.
Run it.

feedback.success: Both environment names changed — and so did the timeout constant.
feedback.why: The substitution matched letters, not structure. It reached the two intended values in one command and renamed an unrelated identifier on the way, which is the cost the repeated structural change avoided.
feedback.contrast: Anchoring the pattern to the quotes would have made this safe; the lesson is that the mechanism only becomes safe once the pattern describes the structure.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: typescript keeps the collateral rename visible on screen next to the two intended changes.

activities.title: Why each call-site edit chose its tool
activities.body: Four edits in one module took four different tools, and none of them was chosen for being short. The quoted value is a structure, so a delimiter text object named it exactly. The trailing argument needed its separator removed with it, so a till-motion drew the range. The swap was movement rather than replacement, so a named register carried the argument past an edit that would have destroyed it. Only the last edit repeated, and only then did a search and a repeat beat describing the change again.
takeaways: Match the tool to the shape of the edit: structure, range, movement, or repetition.
A substitution is the cheapest way to reach every match and the easiest way to reach one you did not want.
Anchor a pattern to the punctuation around a value when a bare word appears elsewhere.
Any delete or change overwrites the unnamed register; name a register before an edit has to survive one.
Repetition earns a search-and-repeat; a single site rarely earns a macro.

lessons.title: Capstone: strings and identifiers
lessons.objective: Rename values and identifiers in one loader, then meet the same edit at a scale where the mechanism has to change.

activities.title: The job among the names
activities.body: A loader holds a quoted value that is wrong, a receiver that was renamed upstream, and a local variable that reads badly in five places. Then the same kind of edit turns up in a log file with far more occurrences than the screen can hold. The commands are all familiar; what changes between the two files is only how many places the edit has to reach.
activities.grammar: how far the edit reaches decides the mechanism, not how clever it is
activities.contrast: A text object rewrites the structure under the cursor; a pattern rewrites every place the text appears, including the ones you were not thinking about.

activities.title: Choose the reach before the rename
activities.prompt: One local variable reads badly in five places inside a seven-line function, and the same letters also appear inside a longer identifier on another line. What fits?

options.label: Search for the whole word, change the first match, and repeat
A file-wide substitution on the bare word
Five separate word changes, one at each site

activities.explanation: Five places is more than is worth typing out and fewer than needs a command line. A whole-word search states which occurrences count, changing the match makes that change repeatable, and each repeat is visible as it lands — so an occurrence inside a longer identifier is never silently swept up. The bare substitution would reach it; five hand edits would work but describe the same change five times.

activities.title: Correct the quoted cache name
activities.instruction: The quoted cache name should read session-cache rather than user-cache. The surrounding assignment stays as it is.

commandGroups.explanation: Change the quoted value as one structure and keep its quotes.
Enter the corrected name.
Return to Normal mode.

checkpoints.caption: The quotes survive; only what they hold is gone.

hints: The value is delimited, so it can be named as a structure rather than counted out.
The cursor does not have to be inside the quotes to change what is between them.
Use `ci"`.

feedback.success: The cache name reads session-cache.
feedback.why: The quoted value is one structure, so a delimiter text object replaced its contents without disturbing the quotes or the assignment.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: python keeps the quoted value and the identifier that shares its letters visible on adjacent lines.

activities.title: Rename the receiver but not its call
activities.instruction: On the assignment line the receiver was renamed upstream and should read store. The attribute access and the argument beside it must survive unchanged.

commandGroups.explanation: Move onto the receiver.
Change the word only, so the punctuation that follows it marks the boundary.
Enter the new name.
Return to Normal mode.

checkpoints.caption: The change stopped at the dot without being told where the dot was.

hints: The receiver ends where the punctuation begins.
One word object respects punctuation as a boundary; the wider one treats the whole run up to the next space as a single word.
Use `ciw`, not `ciW`.

feedback.success: The receiver reads store and its call is untouched.
feedback.why: The narrow word object treats punctuation as a boundary, so the change ended at the dot without a count or a character search.
feedback.contrast: The wider word object would have swallowed the attribute access and its argument as far as the next space.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: python attribute access puts a punctuation boundary immediately after the word being renamed.

activities.title: Rename the local through all five uses
activities.instruction: The local variable should read record at every one of its five uses in this function, and the longer identifier on the second line must keep its own name.

commandGroups.explanation: Search for the whole word under the cursor, so a longer identifier containing it never matches.
Come back to the first use, which the forward search stepped over.
Change this match, which also makes the change repeatable.
Repeat it at each remaining use.

checkpoints.caption: The whole-word search jumped over the longer identifier entirely.
Changing the match is what makes the next repeat find its own target.

hints: Searching for the word under the cursor already anchors the pattern to whole words.
The forward search lands past the first use, so the first change needs a step back.
Change the match with `cgn` and then repeat with `.`.

feedback.success: All five uses read record, and the longer identifier kept its name.
feedback.why: Changing a match rather than a word makes the repeat carry its own search, so each repetition lands on the next real occurrence instead of wherever the cursor happened to be.
feedback.contrast: A plain word change would have repeated only where you moved the cursor yourself.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: python spreads five uses of one local across a function short enough to verify at a glance.

activities.title: Retitle every debug call in the log module
activities.instruction: Every debug call in this module should be a trace call instead. The error calls scattered among them must be left alone, and the module is longer than the window shows.

commandGroups.explanation: Open the command line.
Rewrite the call name across the whole file, reaching the rows below the window as well.
Run it.

feedback.success: Every debug call reads trace, and all four error calls are untouched.
feedback.why: At this many occurrences the edit is uniform and its text is unambiguous, so stating it once reaches the rows past the window at no extra cost. This is the same rename as the last stage, and the change in scale is what changed the tool.
feedback.contrast: Repeating a change here would have meant one visible repetition per row, most of them off screen.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: python log calls repeat one exact token often enough that the mechanism has to change, with untouched neighbours proving the reach was correct.

activities.title: What the unbounded rename would have cost
activities.instruction: Watch the rejected mechanism rename the receiver in the loader and check the other three lines it changed.

commandGroups.explanation: Open the command line.
Rewrite the word everywhere it appears, including inside longer identifiers and inside quoted values.
Run it.

feedback.success: The receiver changed — and so did both uses of the longer identifier and the quoted value.
feedback.why: The pattern matched letters wherever they occurred. In the log module that reach was the whole point; in a seven-line function with one intended site it is three unwanted edits, and the file is short enough that repeating a visible change costs nothing.
feedback.contrast: Anchoring the pattern to whole words would have spared the longer identifier but still rewritten the quoted value, because the hyphen before it is a word boundary too.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: python puts the intended site, a longer identifier, and a quoted value close enough that every consequence is on one screen.

activities.title: Why the same rename took two different tools
activities.body: The last stage and the demonstration ran the same command with the same shape, and only one of them was right. Nothing about the substitution changed between them — the file did. Five occurrences in view, with a lookalike identifier nearby, favour a repeat you can watch land. Ten occurrences spread past the window, with unambiguous text, favour a command that states the edit once. Scale and ambiguity pick the mechanism; neither is a property of the command.
takeaways: Count the occurrences and check whether they fit on screen before choosing.
Prefer a repeat you can watch when a lookalike is nearby; prefer a pattern when the text is unambiguous.
A whole-word anchor still matches inside hyphenated text, so it is not a guarantee of safety.
Changing a match rather than a word makes the repeat find its own next target.
The same command is a good choice and a bad one in two files; judge the file, not the command.

lessons.title: Capstone: formatting and indentation
lessons.objective: Restore the shape of a module and a runbook by matching each formatting fix to the boundary that already describes it.

activities.title: The job with the shapes
activities.body: A helper has been pasted back together: its chain is split across three lines and its body lost a level of indentation. The runbook beside it has a paragraph that runs past the review width and a numbered list where every number is one. None of these edits changes what the code or the prose says — each one restores a shape that something in the file already describes.
activities.grammar: make the range visible or let the file state it, then apply the operator
activities.contrast: A range you address by number is committed before you can see it; a selection and a paragraph both show you what will move first.

activities.title: Choose how to describe the block
activities.prompt: The body of a function has lost a level of indentation. The signature and the closing brace are correct and must not move. What describes the block?

options.label: Select the body lines, check what is highlighted, then indent the selection
A Normal-mode indent run over every line in the file
A counted indent guessed from the number of body lines

activities.explanation: Two of these three edits are committed before you can see what they will touch. A selection shows the exact set of lines first, so an off-by-one is visible while it is still free to fix — and on a phone, where the closing brace may be below the window, that is the difference between a correct indent and a silent one. The file-wide run would move the signature and the closing brace too, and the counted indent is right only until a statement is added.

activities.title: Rejoin the split chain
activities.instruction: The returned chain has been broken across three lines and should sit on one, with no space introduced before either dot.

commandGroups.explanation: Count the three lines the chain occupies.
Join them exactly as written, without inserting the separator a plain join would add.

hints: The chain is three lines, not two.
One join tidies spacing on the way; the other joins the text exactly as it stands.
Use `3gJ`, not `3J`.

feedback.success: The chain sits on one line with both dots tight against their calls.
feedback.why: The join that preserves text exactly is the one that suits code, because the line breaks here sit where a separator would be wrong.
feedback.contrast: A plain join would have produced a space before each dot and broken the chain.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: javascript method chains break across lines exactly where an inserted space would be wrong.

activities.title: Give the body its level back
activities.instruction: Both statements in the function body should sit one level in, and you should be able to see exactly which lines will move before they do. The signature and the closing brace stay where they are.

commandGroups.explanation: Select the two body lines, so the exact range is on screen before anything moves.
Indent what is selected by one level.

checkpoints.caption: Two lines highlighted, and neither brace among them.

hints: The signature and the closing brace must stay where they are.
Seeing the range before committing to it is the point; a selection shows it, a count does not.
Select with `Vj`, then indent with `>`.

feedback.success: The body is one level in and the braces did not move.
feedback.why: The selection put the exact range on screen before the operator ran, so an off-by-one would have been visible while it was still free to fix.
feedback.contrast: A counted indent commits to a number first and shows you the result afterwards.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: javascript braces put an explicit, visible boundary around the lines that need the level.

activities.title: Reflow the runbook paragraph
activities.instruction: The opening paragraph runs past the review width and should be wrapped to it. The numbered list below must keep its own line breaks.

lines: Run each step in order and record the row counts before and after.
Run each step in order and record the

commandGroups.explanation: Reflow to the configured width.
Take the paragraph as the range, so the blank line below stops it short of the list.

lines: Run each step in order and record the

hints: The blank line under the paragraph is already a boundary.
A range of lines would have to be counted; a paragraph object does not.
Use `gqap`.

feedback.success: The paragraph wraps to the review width and the list is untouched.
feedback.why: The paragraph object took its boundary from the blank line, so the reflow stopped exactly where the prose stopped.
feedback.contrast: A counted line range would have needed recounting the moment the paragraph grew, and reaching one line too far would have folded the list into the prose.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: markdown separates prose from a list with a blank line, which is the boundary the paragraph object reads.

activities.title: Renumber the runbook steps
activities.instruction: Every step in the list is numbered one. The second and third steps should read two and three, and the first step keeps its number.

lines: Run each step in order and record the
Run each step in order and record the

commandGroups.explanation: Select the two steps whose numbers are wrong.
Increase each selected number by a step more than the last, turning equal numbers into a sequence.

checkpoints.caption: Two lines selected, and the first step deliberately left out.

lines: Run each step in order and record the

feedback.success: The steps read one, two, three.
feedback.why: The progressive increment gives each selected line a larger increase than the one before, so a column of equal numbers becomes a sequence in one command.
feedback.contrast: The plain increment would have made every selected number two.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: markdown ordered lists are conventionally written with repeated ones, so the repair is a real one.

activities.title: What the blanket indent would have cost
activities.instruction: Watch the rejected mechanism indent the module and check the first and last lines.

commandGroups.explanation: Open the command line.
Run a Normal-mode indent on every line in the file, which is the appeal and the flaw.
Run it.

feedback.success: The body is indented — and so are the signature and the closing brace.
feedback.why: The range was chosen by hand and said every line, while the braces were saying something narrower the whole time. The command is the right one when the line set really is known; here the file already knew a better one.
feedback.contrast: Addressing the body's two lines by number would have worked today and been wrong as soon as a statement was added.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: javascript makes the over-indented signature and closing brace obvious at a glance.

activities.title: Why each shape fix chose its boundary
activities.body: Four formatting fixes, and in three of them the work was choosing the range rather than the operator. A selection and a blank line each made the range visible or let the file state it, so neither edit needed a line count and neither goes stale when a line is added. Only the join counted, because three split lines are a fact about this paste and not a structure. The operators here are the easy part; the boundary is the decision.
takeaways: Prefer a range you can see, or one the file states, over one you count.
A counted range is correct today and wrong after the next line is added.
Choose the join that matches the material: one tidies spacing, the other preserves text exactly.
The progressive increment turns a column of equal numbers into a sequence; the plain one does not.
A file-wide range is the right tool only when the line set genuinely is every line.

lessons.title: Capstone: irregular repeated structures
lessons.objective: Quote the values in a settings block whose keys are all different lengths, and handle the row that does not fit the pattern.

activities.title: The job on rows that do not match
activities.body: Every value in this settings block needs quotes around it. The rows look repetitive and are not: the keys are different lengths, so the separator sits at a different column on every line, and one row in the middle is a bare word with no separator at all. A recording can do all of this, but only if it describes where to go rather than how far.
activities.grammar: anchor to something the row contains, never to a column number
activities.contrast: A column is the same on every row whether or not it means anything; a separator is only ever found where it actually is.

activities.title: Choose what the recording should aim at
activities.prompt: The same two-part edit has to run on rows whose keys are all different lengths, and one row in the block does not have the separator the edit depends on. What should the recording aim at?

options.label: The separator itself, found by a character search inside the recording
The column the separator occupies on the first row
A single substitution across the whole block

activities.explanation: A search inside the recording finds the separator wherever it sits, so rows of different widths are all handled by the same keys — and on the row that has no separator the search simply fails, which ends the run instead of damaging the line. A column is right for the row you recorded on and wrong for the rest. A substitution could add the opening quote or the closing quote, but this edit needs both ends of a value it has to locate first.

activities.title: Quote the first three values
activities.instruction: Wrap the value on each of the first three settings rows in quotation marks, using one recording rather than three separate edits. The keys are different lengths, so the recording has to find the separator on each row.

commandGroups.explanation: Start recording into register a.
Find the separator wherever it sits on this row.
Open the quote immediately after it.
Close the quote at the end of the line.
Step to the next row and return to its start, so a replay begins where this run ended.
Stop recording.
Replay it on the next two rows.

checkpoints.caption: One row done, and the cursor is already parked for the next run.

hints: The keys are different lengths, so nothing about the first row's spacing will hold on the second.
A recording that ends on the next row's first column can be replayed immediately.
Record with `qa`, anchor with `f=`, and finish with `j0` before `q`.

feedback.success: Three values are quoted and the recording is still in the register.
feedback.why: Because the recording searched for the separator instead of counting to it, the same keys fitted rows of three different widths.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: toml settings rows give keys of naturally different lengths, which is what makes the column approach fail.

activities.title: Ask for more runs than the block can take
activities.instruction: Quote the remaining values with a single generous count rather than counting the rows first. The bare word partway down has no separator, and the run should end there with the rows below it untouched.

commandGroups.explanation: Start recording into register a.

commandGroups.display: f= a" Esc A" Esc j0
commandGroups.explanation: Anchor, quote both ends, and advance.
Stop recording.
Ask for nine more runs without counting how many rows can accept one.

checkpoints.caption: One row quoted; nine replays now owed.

hints: The count says how many runs you want, not how many the block can support.
A row without the separator gives the anchor nothing to find.
Use a generous count such as `9@a` and let the block decide.

feedback.success: The run stopped at the bare word, and the two rows below it are untouched.
feedback.why: The anchor failed on a row that does not fit the pattern, so Vim ended that run and cancelled every replay still owed. A generous count is safe precisely because the anchor can fail.
feedback.contrast: A column-anchored recording would have found something at that column and quoted the wrong text nine times over.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: toml makes the bare word among key-value rows an obvious break in the pattern.

activities.title: Reach the rows beyond the bare word
activities.instruction: Two settings rows below the bare word still need quotes. Finish them with one recording that steps over the row without a separator instead of stopping at it.

commandGroups.explanation: Start recording into register a.
Search for the next separator anywhere ahead, which walks past any row that has none.
Quote both ends of the value the search landed on.
Stop recording. The search is the advance, so no separate step is needed.
Replay it on the last row.

checkpoints.caption: The search jumped straight over the bare word.

hints: The previous stage stopped at the bare word; this one has to get past it.
A search finds the next separator wherever it is, so the recording needs no separate step to change rows.
Anchor with `/=` and let it do the advancing.

feedback.success: Both remaining values are quoted and the bare word is untouched.
feedback.why: Searching forward for the anchor makes the irregular row invisible to the recording, because a row without the separator is simply never landed on.
feedback.contrast: The same anchor as a character search stopped the run one stage ago; as a buffer search it skips instead. Whether an odd row halts you or is stepped over is a property of the anchor, not of the row.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: toml keeps the skipped row adjacent to the rows that still need work, so the step over it is visible.

activities.title: Extend a recording that forgot to move
activities.instruction: Quote every value in this second block. Record the edit, and when the recording turns out to have no way of reaching the next row, extend the same register rather than starting again.

commandGroups.display: qa f= a" Esc A" Esc q
commandGroups.explanation: Record the edit, which quotes this row and stays on it.
Reopen the same register in append mode instead of re-recording it.
Add the missing advance to the end of the recording.
Replay the completed recording on the three remaining rows.

checkpoints.caption: The edit is right and the recording cannot repeat: it ends where it started.
The advance is appended, and the cursor has moved with it.

feedback.success: Every value in the block is quoted, from one recording made in two passes.
feedback.why: An uppercase register name appends to what is already recorded, so a recording that is correct but incomplete can be finished rather than redone.
feedback.contrast: Re-recording would have worked too, and would have retyped the part that was already right.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: toml repeats the first block's shape exactly, so the only new thing in this stage is the repair.

activities.title: What the column-anchored recording would have cost
activities.instruction: Watch the rejected mechanism aim at the column the separator occupied on the first row, and check the fourth row.

commandGroups.explanation: Start recording into register a.
Go to the column the separator happens to occupy on this row.
Insert the quote there, whatever is there.
Advance and stop recording.
Replay it three times.

feedback.success: Three rows took the quote where the separator was, and the fourth took it inside the key.
feedback.why: A column exists on every row and means something on only some of them. Nothing failed, nothing warned, and the longest key was quietly cut in half — which is worse than the run that stopped, because a stopped run is visible.
feedback.contrast: The recording is also missing the closing quote everywhere, because a column can locate a position but says nothing about where a value ends.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: toml keys of four and eight characters make the misplaced quote land inside a word rather than near one.

activities.title: Why the recordings aimed at structure
activities.body: The same job met one row that did not fit, and the anchor decided what happened. A character search on the row stopped the run and left the rest of the block visibly undone. A buffer search stepped over the row and finished the job. A column carried on regardless and damaged a key without reporting anything. Two of those are useful answers and the third is the only one that fails silently — which is the property worth choosing against, not the number of rows each one handled.
takeaways: Aim a recording at something the row contains, not at a distance from its start.
A generous count is safe when the anchor can fail, because the failure ends the run.
A character search stops at a row that does not match; a buffer search steps over it.
Prefer a mechanism that fails loudly over one that cannot fail at all.
Append to a register to finish a recording that is right but incomplete.

lessons.title: Capstone: search-driven cleanup
lessons.objective: Retire a value that appears in places it must not be changed, escalating from counting to repeating to confirming to committing.

activities.title: The job among the matches
activities.body: One value has to be retired across an environment file. It also appears in a comment that explains what it meant, and in a key whose own name is that word — neither should change. The commands here are all familiar. What the file asks for is an order of operations: find out how far a pattern reaches before deciding how much of it to trust.
activities.grammar: count, then repeat what you can watch, then confirm what you cannot, then commit
activities.contrast: A count tells you how far a pattern reaches; running it tells you the same thing afterwards.

activities.title: Choose the first move against an unfamiliar file
activities.prompt: A value must be retired throughout a file you have not read closely, and you already suspect some occurrences are legitimate. What comes first?

options.label: Run the pattern in a form that reports its reach and changes nothing
Run the substitution, read the result, and undo it if it went too far
Change the first match and repeat, watching each one land

activities.explanation: Counting costs one command and tells you the size and shape of the job while the buffer is still untouched. Substituting and undoing also works, but it commits before it informs, and on a phone the lines it reached are mostly off screen when you have to judge the result. Repeating from the top is the right tool a step later — once you know how many matches there are and which of them are real.

activities.title: Measure the pattern before using it
activities.instruction: Report how many assignments of the retired value this file contains, without changing a single character. The comment and the key that share the word must not be part of that number.

commandGroups.explanation: Open the command line.
Address the whole file and begin a substitution.
Enter a pattern that includes the separator, so a comment and a key name cannot match it.
Replace it with itself, so nothing can change even if the command runs.
Report the reach instead of applying it.
Run it.

hints: The safest command against an unfamiliar file changes nothing at all.
A substitution can report how far it would reach instead of reaching.
Make the replacement identical to the pattern and add the counting flag.

feedback.success: The count arrived and the file is untouched.
feedback.why: Two decisions were made before anything changed: that the separator belongs in the pattern, and that six matches is a job worth doing in one pass rather than by hand.
feedback.contrast: The same command without the counting flag would have answered the same question by doing the work.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: shell environment files put assignments, a comment, and a key named after its own value in the same short block.

activities.title: Retire the first three assignments
activities.instruction: Change the first three assignments of the retired value so each reads fresh instead, watching every one of them land.

commandGroups.explanation: Search with the same precise pattern the count used.
Change the match itself rather than the text under the cursor, which is what makes the change repeatable.
Repeat it on the next two matches.

checkpoints.caption: The change carried the match with it, so the repeat needs no navigation.

hints: The pattern is already known to be safe; what remains is to apply it where you can see it.
A change aimed at the match rather than at the cursor repeats without any repositioning.
Use `cgn`, then repeat with `.`.

feedback.success: Three assignments read fresh, and every one of them was visible as it changed.
feedback.why: Changing the match rather than a word means each repeat finds its own next target, so the result never depends on where the cursor happened to land.
feedback.contrast: Moving with the search and repeating a word change would have worked here and would have depended on each match sitting in the same relative position.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: shell assignments of differing key length keep the match in a different column on every row.

activities.title: Decline the match that should stay
activities.instruction: The line where the retired word is itself a key name must survive untouched. Put that one line under review and reject the change it offers, without relying on undo afterwards.

commandGroups.explanation: Open the command line.
Address that one line, so nothing else in the file is at risk.
Ask to be shown the match before it changes.
Run it and wait at the prompt.
Decline this match, which ends the run with the line unchanged.

checkpoints.caption: The prompt is waiting, and nothing has changed yet.

hints: This line is the one the pattern was never meant to reach.
A confirming substitution shows a match and waits, so a wrong match costs nothing.
Address the single line and add the confirm flag, then decline.

feedback.success: The line is untouched, and the decision was made before the change rather than after it.
feedback.why: Confirming turns a substitution into a review: the match is shown in place, and declining is free. Undo would also have restored the line, at the cost of first making a change you did not want.
feedback.contrast: Deciding by undo gets harder the moment the command changed several lines, because undo cannot keep the ones that were right.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: shell allows a key whose name is the same word as the value being retired, which is what makes the match legitimate.

activities.title: Commit the pattern you have proved
activities.instruction: Three assignments of the retired value remain, one of them below the window. Finish them in one command, and leave both the comment and the key named after the word exactly as they are.

commandGroups.explanation: Open the command line.
Apply the pattern that was counted, repeated, and reviewed across the whole file.
Run it.

feedback.success: The last three assignments read fresh, and the comment and key name are intact.
feedback.why: Committing in bulk is the cheapest of these mechanisms and the last one to earn its place. By this point the pattern had been counted, watched three times, and reviewed once on the only line where it was wrong.
feedback.contrast: The same command was available at the very start and would have been indistinguishable from a careless one.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: shell keeps the last assignment below the seven-row window, so the command's reach is larger than the evidence on screen.

activities.title: What the unproven pattern would have cost
activities.instruction: Watch the rejected mechanism run the obvious pattern across the file, and read the comment and the sixth line afterwards.

commandGroups.explanation: Open the command line.
Replace the bare word everywhere, which is the command anyone reaches for first.
Run it.

feedback.success: The three real assignments changed — and so did the comment and the key line.
feedback.why: The pattern was never wrong about the assignments; it was wrong about being complete. Dropping the separator widened it by three matches, and nothing in the result says which three were unintended.
feedback.contrast: Counting first would have shown eight matches where the precise pattern showed six, and that difference is the whole warning.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: shell puts the collateral damage in a comment and a key name, both of which still read as valid text afterwards.

activities.title: Why the cleanup escalated instead of committing
activities.body: The last stage and the demonstration are nearly the same command, run on the same file, a few minutes apart. What separates them is evidence. Counting established the size of the job and the shape of a pattern that excluded what it should. Repeating proved the pattern three times where every result was visible. Confirming handled the one line where the pattern was right and the intent was not. Only then was a single command over the whole file the cheap option rather than the reckless one.
takeaways: Count a pattern before trusting it; the command that reports costs no more than the one that acts.
Include the punctuation around a value when the bare word appears in prose or in a name.
Change the match rather than the word when the change has to repeat.
Confirm on a narrow address when a match is legitimate; declining is cheaper than undoing.
A bulk command is earned by evidence, and reads identically whether or not you gathered any.

lessons.title: Capstone: register-preserving refactors
lessons.objective: Move two snippets across a module while deletes happen in between, and choose what protects the text in transit.

activities.title: The job in transit
activities.body: A stray import sits below the function that should never have been under it, and a constant belongs inside the function rather than above it. Neither move is hard on its own. What makes them a capstone is that each one needs something deleted in between, and every delete changes what a plain put would give back. The decision is where the text waits while the rest of the edit happens.
activities.grammar: decide where the text waits before you make the delete that would overwrite it
activities.contrast: A yank or delete without a register name lands in the unnamed one, which the very next delete overwrites; a named register is overwritten only when you name it again.

activities.title: Choose what protects the text in transit
activities.prompt: A line has to be lifted out and put back three lines lower, and a blank line between the two positions has to go first. What keeps the lifted line available?

options.label: Lift the line into a named register and delete the blank into the black hole
Lift the line normally, then count down the numbered registers to find it again
Lift the line normally and put it back from the unnamed register

activities.explanation: The plain unnamed register holds whatever was removed most recently, which after the blank line is the blank line. Counting down the numbered registers does recover the text, but the number depends on how many deletes happened in between, so it is a fact you have to keep in your head and re-derive if the plan changes. Naming the register at the moment you lift the line, and sending the throwaway delete to the black hole, makes both facts explicit and neither of them positional.

activities.title: Hold the stray import somewhere safe
activities.instruction: The import stranded at the bottom of the module has to survive the edits that follow. Put a copy of that whole line somewhere a later delete cannot reach, and leave the module exactly as it is.

commandGroups.explanation: Name the register that will hold the line.
Copy the whole line into it, leaving the buffer untouched.

hints: Nothing in the buffer should change at this stage.
A register name goes in front of the operator, not after it.
Use `"ayy`.

feedback.success: The line is held in a named register and the module is unchanged.
feedback.why: Naming the register at the moment of the copy is what makes the text independent of everything that happens next.
feedback.contrast: Naming a register also means the yank register stays empty — it fills only when a yank does not name one.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: javascript modules put imports at the top by convention, so a stranded one is visibly out of place.

activities.title: Move the stray import into the block
activities.instruction: With the line already held, the stray import should leave the bottom of the module and appear directly under the first import. The removal must not disturb anything that is being held.

commandGroups.explanation: Delete the stray line into the black hole, so no register records it.
Move to the first import.
Put the held line back from its named register, below the current line.

checkpoints.caption: The line is gone from the buffer and every register is exactly as it was.

hints: The line being removed is already held elsewhere, so nothing needs to record it a second time.
One register exists precisely so that a delete leaves no trace.
Delete with `"_dd` and put with `"ap`.

feedback.success: The imports sit together and the held line is still held.
feedback.why: The black hole absorbed the delete, so neither the unnamed register nor the numbered ones shifted, and the put found exactly what was placed there two steps earlier.
feedback.contrast: A plain delete would have overwritten the unnamed register and pushed the numbered ones down by one.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: javascript import order is a real reason to relocate a line rather than retype it.

activities.title: Recover the constant after the deletes
activities.instruction: The constant above the function belongs inside it, and the blank line between them should go too. Remove them both first, then bring the constant back as the first line of the body, indented to match.

commandGroups.explanation: Remove the constant, which the most recent delete register now holds.
Remove the blank line, which pushes the constant one place further down the numbered registers.
Put back the second most recent delete, which is the constant.
Indent the restored line to match the body.

checkpoints.caption: The constant is the most recent delete — for exactly one more keystroke.
The blank line took its place, and the constant moved one slot down.

hints: Each new line delete pushes the previous ones one place further down.
Two deletes happened, so the line you want is not the most recent one.
Put it back with `"2p`.

feedback.success: The constant sits inside the function, indented with the body.
feedback.why: Line deletes fill the numbered registers in order, so text is still recoverable after later deletes — as long as you can say how many happened.
feedback.contrast: The unnamed register held the blank line by then, so a plain put would have inserted an empty line.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: javascript scoping makes moving a constant into the function that uses it a real refactor rather than a rearrangement.

activities.title: Make the same move without needing to count
activities.instruction: Reach the same result as the previous stage — the constant inside the function and indented, the blank line gone — but this time nothing about the outcome should depend on how many deletes happened along the way.

commandGroups.explanation: Remove the constant into a named register, deciding where it waits at the moment it leaves.
Send the throwaway delete to the black hole so it records nothing.
Put the constant back by name, whatever happened in between.
Indent the restored line to match the body.

checkpoints.caption: The black hole recorded nothing at all, so the constant is still exactly where it was put.

feedback.success: Same result, and the put named exactly what it wanted.
feedback.why: Naming the register on the way out and discarding the throwaway delete turns two positional facts into two stated ones, so the sequence still reads correctly if a third delete is added tomorrow.
feedback.contrast: The recovery in the previous stage was correct, but its register number was true only for that exact number of deletes.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: javascript repeats the previous stage's refactor exactly, so only the method differs between them.

activities.title: What the unprotected move would have cost
activities.instruction: Watch the rejected mechanism make the same two removals and put back whatever the unnamed register happens to hold.

commandGroups.explanation: Remove the constant into the unnamed register.
Remove the blank line, which overwrites the unnamed register without warning.
Put back whatever the unnamed register holds now.

checkpoints.caption: The unnamed register holds the constant.
The unnamed register holds the blank line, and nothing said so.

feedback.success: A blank line came back instead of the constant, and the buffer looks almost right.
feedback.why: The unnamed register is overwritten by every delete, so the put returned the most recent one. The failure is quiet: no error, no warning, and a module that still parses.
feedback.contrast: The constant was not lost — it was one slot down the numbered registers the whole time. Recovery was possible; noticing was the hard part.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: javascript still parses after the wrong line is restored, which is what makes the failure quiet.

activities.title: Why the moves named their registers
activities.body: Three routes reached the same constant: the unnamed register, which was wrong; a numbered register, which was right but only for that exact number of deletes; and a named register, which was right regardless. None of them differed much in length. What differed was how much of the outcome lived in your head. Naming the register on the way out costs two keys and removes the need to remember anything at all — and the black hole is the matching half, because a delete that records nothing cannot disturb what you are protecting.
takeaways: Decide where text waits at the moment you remove it, not when you need it back.
Every delete overwrites the unnamed register, and the failure is silent.
Numbered registers make text recoverable, at the cost of counting the deletes since.
Send a throwaway delete to the black hole so it disturbs no register at all.
A yank that names a register leaves the yank register empty; a yank that does not, fills it.
Prefer the method that stays correct when a step is added tomorrow.

lessons.title: Capstone: predicate-based batch editing
lessons.objective: Triage a build plan longer than the window by describing which lines qualify rather than where they sit.

activities.title: The job across a plan you cannot see
activities.body: A build plan runs past the bottom of the window. Some of its steps are deferred, and those need marking, collecting, and telling apart from the steps that still run. Every line number you could write down here stops being true the moment a line moves — and the first thing this job does is move lines. What stays true is what each line says about itself.
activities.grammar: select lines by what they contain, then give the selection one command to run
activities.contrast: A numeric range is a fact about the file as it is now; a predicate is a fact about the lines themselves.

activities.title: Choose how to name the lines
activities.prompt: The same short edit must run on the deferred steps of a plan that is longer than the window, and an earlier command in the same session has already moved lines around. What names them?

options.label: A predicate matching what the deferred lines say
A numeric range covering the rows they occupied
A recorded macro replayed with a generous count

activities.explanation: Membership here depends on the text, not the position, and the positions have already changed once. A predicate re-derives the set every time it runs, so it cannot go stale and does not need the rows to be adjacent or on screen. A numeric range would have to be re-read from a file that does not fit the window. A macro could do the edit but would have to be steered to each row, which is the part the predicate does for free.

activities.title: Mark every deferred step
activities.instruction: Each deferred step should end with a note reading (later). They are scattered through the plan and some are below the window, and the steps that still run must not be touched.

commandGroups.explanation: Open the command line.
Select every line that announces itself as deferred, wherever it sits.
Give that selection one Normal-mode edit to run on each of its lines.
Run it.

hints: The deferred steps are not adjacent and not all visible.
Anchor the predicate to the start of the line so it cannot match the word elsewhere.
Use `:g/^skip/normal A (later)`.

feedback.success: All four deferred steps carry the note, including the ones below the window.
feedback.why: The predicate found the lines by what they say, so their scattering and the window's size were both irrelevant to writing the command.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: log build plans naturally interleave steps that run with steps that are skipped.

activities.title: Collect the deferred steps at the end
activities.instruction: The deferred steps should sit together after the whole plan instead of interrupting it, keeping the order they already have.

commandGroups.explanation: Open the command line.
Select the same lines again — the predicate did not need updating after the last edit.
Move each matching line to the end, one at a time in the order they are found.
Run it.

hints: The command a predicate runs does not have to edit text; it can be an address-taking command.
Moving each match to the end, in the order they are found, preserves their relative order.
Use `:g/^skip/m$`.

feedback.success: The four deferred steps sit together at the end, still in their original order.
feedback.why: Because each match is moved to the end as it is found, the last one found ends up last, so a relocation to a fixed final address preserves order rather than reversing it.
feedback.contrast: Relocating each match to the top instead would have reversed them, for exactly the same reason.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: log rows carry a visible sequence, so a reversal would be obvious if the relocation caused one.

activities.title: Comment out everything that is not a running step
activities.instruction: Only the steps that still run should remain live. Every other line — the two plan headings and the deferred block now at the end — should be commented out, in one pass.

commandGroups.explanation: Open the command line.
Select every line that does not match, which is far easier to state than the six lines that do.
Comment each selected line at its start.
Run it.

hints: The lines to keep share a prefix; the lines to change have nothing in common with each other.
A predicate can be inverted, so the easier half to describe is the one you write.
Use `:v/^step/` rather than trying to name the six lines.

feedback.success: Every heading and every deferred step is commented, and the running steps are untouched.
feedback.why: Two headings and four deferred rows have no shared text, but their complement does. Inverting the predicate turned an impossible description into a four-character one.
feedback.contrast: Describing the six lines positively would have needed an alternation of two patterns, and would have broken the next time a heading was reworded.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: log gives the running steps one shared prefix and the remaining lines none, which is what makes inversion the cheaper description.

activities.title: Stamp every running step as checked
activities.instruction: The prepared recording in register a marks one line as checked. Every running step should carry that mark, and nothing else in the plan should change.

commandGroups.explanation: Open the command line.
Select the running steps.
Run the recording once on each selected line, rather than steering it there by hand.
Run it.

feedback.success: All ten running steps are marked, and the commented lines are untouched.
feedback.why: The predicate chose the lines and the recording described the edit, so neither had to know anything about the other. A macro that would otherwise need a count and a safe stopping condition needs neither once something else decides where it runs.
feedback.contrast: Replaying the recording with a count would have walked into the commented block and marked it too.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: log keeps the running steps in one contiguous block with commented lines above and below, so an over-reach would be visible immediately.

activities.title: What the numeric range would have cost
activities.instruction: Watch the rejected mechanism reuse the rows the deferred steps occupied before they were moved, then watch a single undo answer for all of it.

commandGroups.explanation: Open the command line.
Delete the rows the deferred steps used to span, before the gather moved them.
Run it.
Undo the whole run with one keystroke.

checkpoints.caption: Ten lines gone, seven of them steps that still had to run.

feedback.success: Ten lines were deleted and one undo brought all of them back.
feedback.why: The addresses were correct when they were written and wrong two commands later, because the gather moved every line below it. A predicate would have re-derived the set at the moment it ran.
feedback.contrast: The recovery is the reassuring half: a whole command counts as one change, so one undo reverses it however many lines it touched. Ten separate hand edits would have cost ten.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: log rows moved by an earlier stage make the staleness concrete rather than hypothetical.

activities.title: Why the plan was addressed by what it says
activities.body: Four commands ran over a file longer than the window, and not one of them named a line number. That was not a stylistic preference: the second command moved every line below it, which would have invalidated any address written before it. A predicate is re-evaluated each time it runs, so it survives its own side effects. The inversion is the same idea pushed one step further — when the lines you want share nothing, describe the ones you do not want.
takeaways: Select by what a line contains when membership depends on text, or when earlier edits move rows.
Anchor a predicate to the line start so it cannot match the same word mid-line.
A predicate can drive a relocation, not only an edit; matches moved to a final address keep their order.
Invert the predicate when the complement is the easier half to describe.
Let the predicate choose the lines and a recording describe the edit; neither needs to know the other.
One command is one change, so one undo reverses the whole run however far it reached.

lessons.title: Capstone: review and surgical correction
lessons.objective: Correct several sites in a checklist longer than the window, returning to each one without searching for it again.

activities.title: The job you keep having to come back to
activities.body: A release checklist runs to twenty lines behind a seven-row window. Several entries are wrong, and each correction needs something checked elsewhere in the file first. The corrections themselves are trivial. What costs time is getting back — and searching your way back is how you end up editing a line that merely looks like the one you meant.
activities.grammar: leave yourself a way back before you go, or ask the editor where you have already been
activities.contrast: A search finds a line that matches; a mark finds the line you were standing on.

activities.title: Choose how to get back
activities.prompt: You are about to leave a line you will need to edit in a moment, and several other lines in the file contain the same words. What gets you back to it?

options.label: Set a mark on the line before leaving it
Search for the line's text when you need it again
Note the line number and address it later

activities.explanation: A mark records the position itself, so it is exact even when several lines read alike, and it survives edits above it that would shift a line number. Searching back finds the first line that matches, which is a different line from the one you meant as soon as the file repeats itself. A remembered number is right until anything above it is added or removed — and the first correction you make may well do that.

activities.title: Leave a mark, check the end, come back
activities.instruction: The status entry still reads draft and should read ready, but only once you have checked the end of the checklist. Leave yourself a way back to this line, read the last line, return, and make the correction.

commandGroups.explanation: Record this exact position under a name before leaving it.
Jump to the last line, far below the window.
Return to the recorded position, column and all.
Move onto the value.
Make the correction now that you are back on the right line.

checkpoints.caption: Nothing has changed and nothing has moved; the position is simply recorded.
Back on the same line and the same column, with no searching involved.

hints: Record the position before you leave, not after.
The exact form of the return puts you back on the column you left, not just the line.
Set the mark with `ma` and return with the backtick form.

feedback.success: The status entry reads ready, corrected from exactly where you left off.
feedback.why: A mark stores a position rather than a pattern, so returning to it cannot land on a similar line somewhere else.
feedback.contrast: The apostrophe form of the same mark would have returned to the line but given up the column.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: prose checklist entries repeat their vocabulary, which is what makes a positional return worth more than a textual one.

activities.title: Come back to where you last edited
activities.instruction: The audit entry should read done. After correcting it, check the checklist heading, then return to the correction and give the entry below it the same treatment — without setting a mark for it.

commandGroups.explanation: Correct the audit entry.
Jump to the heading to check it.
Return to the position of the last change, which Vim recorded without being asked.
Step down to the next entry and onto its value.
Correct that one too.

checkpoints.caption: Back at the edit, with no mark set and nothing searched for.

hints: The editor already remembers where you last changed something.
There is a mark you never have to set, and it updates itself with every edit.
Return with the backtick form of the last-change mark.

feedback.success: Both entries read done, and the return cost two keystrokes and no preparation.
feedback.why: Vim maintains a mark at the last change automatically, so a return to the site of your own most recent edit never needs setting up in advance.
feedback.contrast: A named mark would have worked identically here and would have had to be placed before the edit — which means predicting that you would leave.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: prose entries sitting next to each other make the second correction a short step from the returned position.

activities.title: Walk back through what you just changed
activities.instruction: Correct the upload and announce entries so both read done, then step back through the two corrections you just made to review them, ending on the earlier of the two.

commandGroups.explanation: Correct the upload entry.
Step down to the announce entry.
Correct that one too.
Step back to the most recent change.
Step back again to the one before it.

checkpoints.caption: The first step back lands on the more recent of the two edits.

hints: The last-change mark only remembers one place; this needs the list behind it.
Each step walks one entry further back through the changes you made.
Step back with `g;`, twice.

feedback.success: Both entries read done, and you finished standing on the earlier of the two corrections.
feedback.why: Vim keeps a list of change positions, not just the latest one, so a review pass can walk backwards through a session's edits in the order they were made.
feedback.contrast: The last-change mark would have returned to the second correction and offered no way to reach the first.

provenance.languageRationale: prose entries corrected in sequence give the change list two entries whose order is unambiguous.

activities.title: Finish the note you were interrupted in
activities.instruction: The approver entry needs a note reading review appended after it. Begin the note, break off to check the heading, then carry on typing exactly where you stopped rather than finding the spot again.

commandGroups.explanation: Start the note at the end of the entry and break off.
Jump to the heading.
Re-enter Insert mode exactly where the last insertion stopped.
Finish the word and leave Insert mode.

checkpoints.caption: Insert mode resumed mid-word, with no repositioning of any kind.

feedback.success: The approver entry reads review, typed in two halves either side of a trip to the top of the file.
feedback.why: Vim records where insertion last stopped and can put you back into Insert mode there, so an interrupted edit resumes rather than restarting.
feedback.contrast: Returning by mark would have reached the line and still needed the cursor placed at the exact character and Insert mode re-entered.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: prose lets the note be split mid-word, which is what makes resuming visibly different from returning.

activities.title: What searching your way back would have cost
activities.instruction: Watch the rejected mechanism search the checklist from the top for a pending entry, then check which entry it corrected.

commandGroups.explanation: Search for the word that identified the entry you meant.
Correct what the search landed on.

checkpoints.caption: The search stopped at the first match, which is not the entry that needed changing.

feedback.success: An entry now reads done — the notes entry, four lines above the audit entry that was meant.
feedback.why: Five entries in this checklist say pending. A search finds the first one, and it looks exactly as correct afterwards as the right one would have. Nothing failed and nothing warned.
feedback.contrast: A mark records the position rather than the words, so repetition in the file cannot mislead it.

provenance.languageRationale: prose checklists repeat status words across many entries, which is exactly the condition that makes a textual return unsafe.

activities.title: Why the returns were positional
activities.body: Four corrections in a file with five identical status words, and not one return was made by searching. Two of the marks had to be set — one by hand before leaving, one by Vim at the moment of the edit — and two were lists Vim was already keeping. The choice between them is only ever about how far ahead you knew you would need to come back: a named mark for a place you are about to leave, the last-change mark for the edit you just made, the change list for a review pass, and the insert position for a sentence you were part-way through.
takeaways: Record a position before leaving it when the file repeats itself; a search finds the first match, not your line.
The last-change mark needs no preparation and is exact for the edit you just made.
The change list walks back through a session's edits when one remembered place is not enough.
Resuming insertion is not the same as returning to a line: it restores the exact character too.
A line number is the one form of return that the next edit above it can invalidate.

reference.purpose: Pick between a structural change, a bounded range, a protected move, and a repeat when editing argument lists.
notes: read the shape of the edit, then pick the tool that matches it
A substitution rewrites matching text anywhere; a text object rewrites one structure exactly where you are standing.

reference.purpose: Choose between a structural change, a repeated match change, and a file-wide substitution when renaming values and identifiers.
notes: how far the edit reaches decides the mechanism, not how clever it is
A text object rewrites the structure under the cursor; a pattern rewrites every place the text appears, including the ones you were not thinking about.

reference.purpose: Match a formatting operator to a range you can see or one the file already states.
notes: make the range visible or let the file state it, then apply the operator
A range you address by number is committed before you can see it; a selection and a paragraph both show you what will move first.

reference.command: qa f= … j0 q · 9@a · qa /=↵ … q · qA
reference.purpose: Anchor a recording to structure so rows of different shapes stop or skip predictably.
notes: anchor to something the row contains, never to a column number
A column is the same on every row whether or not it means anything; a separator is only ever found where it actually is.

reference.purpose: Establish what a pattern reaches before deciding how much of it to run at once.
notes: count, then repeat what you can watch, then confirm what you cannot, then commit
A count tells you how far a pattern reaches; running it tells you the same thing afterwards.

reference.purpose: Keep a snippet available across the deletes that a relocation needs.
notes: decide where the text waits before you make the delete that would overwrite it
A yank or delete without a register name lands in the unnamed one, which the very next delete overwrites; a named register is overwritten only when you name it again.

reference.purpose: Select lines by what they contain and give the selection one command to run.
notes: select lines by what they contain, then give the selection one command to run
A numeric range is a fact about the file as it is now; a predicate is a fact about the lines themselves.

reference.command: ma then backtick-a · backtick-dot · g; · gi
reference.purpose: Return to a site you have to correct without searching for it again.
notes: leave yourself a way back before you go, or ask the editor where you have already been
A search finds a line that matches; a mark finds the line you were standing on.
